text:
I personally feel that math and problem solving is something that every human needs some amount of. This is true for any career. 

So there will be a need for teaching. But I wonder what level of teaching is necessary for problem solving. 

As someone who learned math through engineering, most of the mathematics here were focused on helping solve some common problems encountered in industries, and the corresponding theory before it to get a grasp. I appreciated the insights and also the knowledge to actually make use of these things in practice. 
But I wonder if these sorts of math teaching will continue to have as much value when u can just ask an Ai to calculate something through whatever numerical method. 
In theory an engineer will not need to know exactly how the calculator works as long as they can understand the results. But they should have some sort of grounding in reality and an intuition to help them catch mistakes from Ais, and the domain knowledge to put these results into use. 

Calculators have been a thing for ages, yet every child is taught how to do basic math since their early childhood. This to me is because its not about knowing what 5x3 is supposed to be, but to build intuition of quantites, numbers and other fundamentals of the world. 
Just because Ai is doing some proofs does not mean that people will not need to learn math. But this also meant that there existed jobs in the past that were purely computational. People doing math by hand was a job, I heard women were quite good at this. This sort of job kinda stopped existing. 


Its really hard to draw a line here on whats necessary to know and what's just a means to practical usage.
For a hypothetical person who is pursuing pure math, their path forward is unchanged, whereas someone from an application perspective may see a decline in math focus and education. As for their job opportunities, its going to remain unchanged, unless the teaching space gets taken over by AI somehow. But at that point half the incentive/career opportunity to study math will go down leading to math being more of a side thing. 

Here is also where the joy and satisfaction part comes in. 
I am now completely disjoint from math as a whole career wise. But I make use of math and my critical thinking in every aspect of my life. Be it in my hobby games, my daily conversations or just being able to watch math, science and other related videos and be able to appreciate them. Interacting with math keeps my mind sharp and cunning(optimizing).

text:
I feel like this video just scoots around the issues AI poses for the process of "Building problem-solving muscles." But while, yes fine, AI cannot stop humans from learning to problem solve through solving mathematical problems, the problem AI poses is that it disincentivises the exercises needed to build those muscles and permits humans to make shortcuts along the way that allows people to solve problems without effort. The effect is likely that, in the long run, human society collectively will confer less value to the people who build problem-solving muscle. And the effect of that is that people as a collective become less intelligent and less capable of complex problem-solving. To some extent this can already be observed in most developed Western countries where basic maths and literacy metrics have been declining for about 10 years, a trend that has been exacerbated since the proliferation of LLMs. 

This also relates to another version of an AI future that this video doesn't engage with. The video supposes that AI will advance ahead of humans in mathematical ability purely through improvements to AI. However, AI may advance ahead of humans because both AI improves AND humans become worse. This, in my opinion, is particularly pertinent when consider the ability to pose interesting conjectures/ask questions and build theories. Especially, if there are less incentives for people to put in the effort to actually build problem-solving muscles, which the video assumes as given can always and will always be done.

In terms of the threats that the use of LLMs/AI poses to humanity, this degradation of the things that are worth valuing in people is the one that poses the most civilisational threat. We shouldn't never assume the trajectory of history necessarily follows a natural tendency towards improvement and progress.

Despite all the noise right now, I still feel like we are living in a golden age of AI. 

The tools have become immensely powerful very quickly - and so you can experience the exhilaration of having a great thinking partner close at hand or suddenly being able to build your own software. And - critically - there is still enough cognitive space for people to step into. 

In your example, LLMs can act as proof machines - but we can step up into conjecture or theory. It’s the 21st century version of people moving out of farms and factories and into offices. 

But there is a plausible future where they become better than us at all cognitive tasks - and that is what scares me. What if there is no brain space left to step into? 

At that point, I don’t think you “still need someone to see how the theory gets applied in surrounding fields”. I think you just have agents talking to one another, whilst we watch from the sidelines.

The worrying prospect is if we end up irrelevant, reduced to hoping that the models stay aligned enough to explain all their great ideas. 

That and an AI apocalypse 😂.

I've taken part in some vaguely analogous conversations about programming and AI lately, and in those, commenters seem to be split roughly into two camps of either, 'I code in order to realise ideas' or, 'I code because I want to code'. In the first case, AI is a positive, because the end goal is the programme/product and AI can (often, though not always) reach that faster/simpler than the human developer (who primarily wants to 1. ideate and 2. realise the idea), whereas in the second case, AI is a negative, because it takes away the part of the process that is, in some sense, its core purpose.

I feel like this video, as well as the one that Matt Parker's posted on OpenAI's Navier Stokes proof, fall rather neatly into the _process above result_ side of that conversation (which is where I fall, both with programming and maths). Your two videos have made me see very clearly in what concrete ways the AI problem/opportunity is both similar and very different between the fields of programming and mathematics and thus, I suppose, the major core ways in which those fields differ over-all as well.
